safetyNote: Do not eat raw or casually cooked Lactarius torminosus: its intensely acrid latex can cause gastrointestinal illness. The Belgian Poison Centre includes this milkcap (spelled 'L. terminosus' in its brochure) among causes of a mild gastrointestinal syndrome. Finland's Food Authority nevertheless recognises a traditional food use after a specific 10-minute boiling and discarding of the water. This regional practice does not make an uncertain identification or ordinary cooking safe; seek local expert guidance and follow local food advice.

sections.title: Pink cap with a woolly rim
sections.text: The cap is usually about 4–12 cm across, convex at first, then flatter and centrally depressed. Its pale salmon-pink to pink-buff surface shows darker concentric zones, with a conspicuous shaggy or bearded fringe on the strongly inrolled young margin. The centre may be relatively smooth and the hairs wear away as the mushroom ages; a faded old cap is therefore less distinctive.

sections.title: Pale gills, hollowing stem and white milk
sections.text: The narrow, crowded gills are pale flesh-pink to cream and broadly attached to shortly decurrent. A cut or broken gill releases white to cream latex that does not change colour in air and is intensely acrid. Do not taste unidentified fungi to test this character. The pale pinkish stem is roughly cylindrical, initially solid or stuffed and later hollow; young stems may be finely downy. Flesh is pale, brittle and unchanged on cutting. The spore deposit is pale cream.

sections.title: Birch association and lookalikes
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal milkcap grows with birch, including in mixed woods and heathland with birches, and fruits mainly from late summer into autumn. The paler L. pubescens, absent from this catalogue, can also have a hairy margin and white latex. Orange milkcaps such as L. deliciosus or L. deterrimus lack the bearded rim and initially exude orange latex. The tree association and fresh latex colour should be checked together with the whole cap.

sections.title: Different regional food guidance
sections.text: The Belgian Poison Centre associates acrid milkcaps including this species with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea typically beginning within three hours of ingestion. In contrast, the Finnish Food Authority lists it among food mushrooms only with a defined pre-boil and disposal of the cooking water; it notes that central and southern Europe often regard it as unsuitable for food. This app marks it toxic to discourage casual consumption, while acknowledging that documented regional preparation practice. If ingestion is followed by symptoms, contact a poison centre promptly.

traits: Salmon-pink to pink-buff cap, roughly 4–12 cm, with darker concentric zones
Strongly inrolled young margin bearing conspicuous long woolly hairs; hairs may wear off in age
Crowded pale pink to cream gills, attached to shortly decurrent
White or cream latex that remains pale in air; intensely acrid
Pale cylindrical stem, sometimes downy when young, hollowing with age; pale brittle flesh
Grows with birch in woodland or heath, mainly late summer to autumn
